etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin approximatus, past participle of approximare (“to approach”); ad + proximare (“to come near”). See proximate.

definitions.definition: Nearing correctness; nearly exact; not perfectly accurate.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Sir Michael Holden, “Reform of the workforce or death by a thousand cuts?”, in RAIL, number 948, page 22:
quote.text: As yet, we don't know what the comparable figures will be like for the current financial year which ends in March 2022, but we can have a good stab at approximating them.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To come near to; to approach.

quote.citation: 1911, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, The Disappearance of Lady Frances Carfax:
quote.text: When you follow two separate chains of thought, Watson, you will find some point of intersection which should approximate to the truth.

quote.citation: 1802, Jedidiah Morse, The American Universal Geography:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To carry or advance near; to cause to approach.

quote.citation: 1790 November, Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, and on the Proceedings in Certain Societies in London Relative to that Event. […], London:  […]  J[ames] Dodsley, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: to approximate the inequality of riches to the level of nature
